### Why testing matters

**NORA:** Let's talk about the customer problem. Why does an aerospace company send its metal to an outside lab?

**JAMES:** A few reasons. First, requirements. In aerospace and defence, materials have to meet tight specifications, and the people buying the parts want independent evidence. A supplier saying our alloy is fine isn't enough. An accredited third party has to test it and certify the result.

**NORA:** Second?

**JAMES:** Second, equipment and expertise. The instruments are expensive and need specialists to run and maintain them. A mid-sized parts maker or a powder producer doesn't want to own a full chemistry and metallurgy lab, keep it accredited, and employ the experts. It's cheaper and more credible to send samples out.

**NORA:** And third?

**JAMES:** Third, the chain of trust. Think of the aerospace supply chain as layers. Raw material producers, then companies that make powder or bar or forgings, then machine shops and component makers, then the big manufacturers who assemble aircraft and engines. At each step, someone wants proof the material is right. The test report travels with the material through that chain.

**NORA:** So the report is effectively part of the product.

**JAMES:** That's exactly how I'd put it. For the customer, the report isn't a nice-to-have. It's what lets them ship. No accepted report, no shipment, no invoice.

**NORA:** What happens if a result turns out to be wrong?

**JAMES:** That's the nightmare scenario, and it explains why customers are so careful. As general background, if material that doesn't meet specification gets into an aerospace part, and it's discovered later, you can face recalls, grounded components, investigations up and down the supply chain, and enormous cost. The test report is one of the places where the industry tries to catch problems before they travel. So a lab's reputation rests on never being the weak link.

**NORA:** So a lab is really selling confidence.

**JAMES:** Confidence and traceability. If a question ever comes up, the lab has to be able to show exactly which sample was tested, on which instrument, calibrated when, by whom, using which method, and what the raw data said. That audit trail is part of what customers are paying for, even if they never look at it.

**NORA:** What does a customer care about most, then?

**JAMES:** In my view, four things. First, that the result is right and defensible, because if it's challenged later, the consequences are severe. Second, that the lab holds the accreditations their customer requires. Third, turnaround time, because a lot of production is waiting on that report. And fourth, ease of doing business. How easy is it to get a quote, send the samples, track progress and get the paperwork in the format they need.

**NORA:** Price isn't on the list?

**JAMES:** Price matters, but in my view it comes after those four for most aerospace work. A cheap result that isn't accepted, or arrives late and holds up a production line, is very expensive. That's partly why switching labs is hard. Customers have qualified NSL, their own customers have accepted NSL's reports, and changing lab means re-qualifying. That's our inference, but it fits how the industry works.

**NORA:** And the newer markets, batteries, additive manufacturing?

**JAMES:** Those are interesting because they're still building their standards. In additive manufacturing, you're printing metal parts from powder, and the industry is still working out how to qualify those powders and parts consistently. NSL's website references the ASTM additive manufacturing centre of excellence and industry user group events, which suggests it's active in that standards community. ASTM is one of the big standards bodies. Being close to where the methods get defined is a real advantage for a lab.

### Inside the lab

**NORA:** Let's go inside. What actually happens when a sample arrives?

**JAMES:** In general terms, it starts with intake. The customer fills in a request, describes the material, the tests they need and the specification it has to meet. On NSL's website, that's a web request form and downloadable sample submission forms. The sample is logged, labelled, and given an identity that follows it through the lab.

**NORA:** Why does that identity matter so much?

**JAMES:** Chain of custody. In general terms, an accredited lab has to be able to prove that the result on the report came from the sample the customer sent, not from a mix-up on the bench. So samples are tracked from the moment they arrive, through preparation, testing and storage. Labs often retain part of the sample for a period, in case a result needs to be checked again. All of that is routine, but it's labour, and it's mostly recorded in systems and on paper.

**NORA:** And preparation?

**JAMES:** Often a big step. A piece of metal may need cutting, cleaning, dissolving in acid for chemical analysis, or mounting and polishing for microscopy. Powders need careful handling. Get the preparation wrong and the instrument faithfully measures the wrong thing. That's skilled work, and it's one reason a lab is not just a room full of machines.

**NORA:** Then the instruments.

**JAMES:** Right. NSL lists a range of them. I'll explain a few. ICP, which stands for inductively coupled plasma, is used to measure which elements are in a material and at what concentration, down to very small amounts. XRF, X-ray fluorescence, is another way of identifying elemental composition. XRD, X-ray diffraction, tells you about the crystal structure, which phases are present. And LCMS-MS, liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry, is used for identifying and measuring chemical compounds, often organic ones.

**NORA:** That's a lot of acronyms.

**JAMES:** It is, and I'll stop there. The important point is that each instrument produces data, numbers, spectra, readings, and that data has to be checked, interpreted against the right method and specification, and turned into a result.

**NORA:** And on the metallurgy side?

**JAMES:** There it's more physical. Cutting and polishing samples, looking at them under microscopes, measuring hardness, running mechanical tests that pull or bend or fatigue a specimen. Again, the output is data and images that a qualified person interprets.

**NORA:** Then the report.

**JAMES:** Then the report. Typically a certificate of analysis or a test report that lists the sample, the methods, the results, whether it meets the specification, and the signature of an authorised person. For accredited work, the format and the review process are controlled. Every number has to trace back to the raw data, and the method has to be the one the lab is accredited for.

**NORA:** Where does the time go in that process?

**JAMES:** We don't have NSL-specific numbers, so this is general industry background. The instrument run is often not the longest step. Sample preparation takes time. Data review takes time. And report writing, especially for complex jobs or customers who want results in their own format, can take a surprising amount of skilled labour. Plus there's administration: quoting, chasing missing information on the request form, answering, where's my result?

**NORA:** And that's where AI comes in.

**JAMES:** That's where we'll come back to it. But first I want to talk about the moat, because it shapes everything.

### The accreditation moat

**NORA:** You keep coming back to accreditation. Explain it for someone who's never worked in a lab.

**JAMES:** Accreditation is an independent body checking that a lab is competent to do specific tests, and keeps checking. NSL lists several. ISO slash IEC 17025 is the international standard for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories. It covers everything from staff training to equipment calibration to how results are reported. Nadcap is an accreditation programme run for the aerospace and defence industry, and many aerospace manufacturers require their suppliers' special processes and labs to have it.

**NORA:** And the others?

**JAMES:** NQA-1 is a quality assurance standard for the nuclear industry. If you want to test materials going into nuclear applications, you need to work under that kind of programme, which explains the nuclear content on the website. And NSL also lists compliance with ITAR and EAR. ITAR is the US International Traffic in Arms Regulations, and EAR is the Export Administration Regulations. They control who can access certain defence and technology data. A lab that handles defence work has to protect that data and control who sees it.

**NORA:** So why is that a moat?

**JAMES:** Because it takes years and a lot of money to build, and it has to be maintained continuously. A new lab can buy instruments. It can't buy a long track record of passing audits, or the trust of aerospace customers who've accepted its reports for years. In my view, the accreditation stack is NSL's most important asset after its people.

**NORA:** And how does it shape the AI question?

**JAMES:** In two ways. First, anything AI touches in the testing process has to fit inside the accredited quality system. You can't just bolt on a tool that changes how results are calculated or reported without validating it. Second, the ITAR and EAR side means data handling is serious. You can't casually send defence-related test data to a cloud AI service without knowing exactly where it goes and who can see it.

**NORA:** So the moat protects NSL but also slows it down.

**JAMES:** That's a fair summary. It's a constraint, but in my view it's also an opportunity. A lab that figures out how to use AI inside a fully accredited, export-controlled environment would have something competitors find hard to copy. The careful way is the defensible way.

### A sample's journey

**NORA:** Let's make it concrete. Give me a hypothetical customer and walk me through it, today and with AI. Invented example, not a real company.

**JAMES:** Let's say there's a company in the Midwest that makes metal powder for 3D printing aerospace parts. We'll call the quality manager Priya. Every production lot of powder needs chemistry testing before it can ship to her customer, an engine parts maker. Her customer's specification lists maximum levels for oxygen, nitrogen and a set of trace elements, and requires a Nadcap-accredited lab.

**NORA:** So what does Priya do today?

**JAMES:** She emails NSL or fills in the web form asking for a quote for the usual test package. Someone at the lab checks the specification and the methods, works out the price and turnaround, and emails a quote. Priya approves it, fills in the sample submission form, prints it, packs the samples and ships them. When the samples arrive, the lab logs them and, if something's missing on the form, someone emails her to ask.

**NORA:** And then she waits.

**JAMES:** She waits. Her shipment to the engine maker is on hold until the report arrives. A couple of days in, she emails to ask how it's going. Someone at the lab checks with the chemists and replies. The tests run. A chemist reviews the data. Someone prepares the certificate, cross-checks every value against the instrument output and the specification, and an authorised person signs it. It arrives as a document by email. Priya's team then types the key values into their own quality system.

**NORA:** Lots of emails.

**JAMES:** Lots of emails, lots of re-typing on both sides. Now let's replay it. Priya logs into a client portal. She picks the test package she always orders for this alloy, and the system gives her an instant quote with standard turnaround and a rush option. She enters the lot details, and the portal checks they're complete before she ships. She prints a label with a code that the lab scans on arrival.

**NORA:** And inside the lab?

**JAMES:** The instruments run as before. But when the results come off the instruments, they flow into the lab's system automatically, and an assistant drafts the certificate. It pulls the values, applies the right specification limits, flags anything close to a limit or out of the usual range for this customer's lots, and lays it out in the required format. The chemist reviews the draft, checks the flags, and the authorised person signs. Nothing goes out without human sign-off.

**NORA:** So the human still owns the result.

**JAMES:** Absolutely. That's non-negotiable in accredited work. What changes is that the human spends their time on judgement rather than on copying numbers into a template. And meanwhile Priya can see the status in the portal, received, testing, under review, issued, without sending an email.

**NORA:** And at the end?

**JAMES:** She gets the signed certificate and the data in a structured file that loads straight into her quality system. Her shipment leaves a day earlier, perhaps. Over a year, across many lots, that adds up for her. And for NSL, faster report issue means faster invoicing, which helps cash flow.

**NORA:** Is there a second-order benefit?

**JAMES:** In my view, yes. Once NSL holds years of structured results for Priya's lots, it can offer insight. Your oxygen levels have been drifting up over the last ten lots. That turns a testing vendor into something closer to a quality partner. That's a stickier relationship and, potentially, a premium service.

**NORA:** Let's do one more, from inside the lab. A day in the life of an invented lab manager.

**JAMES:** Let's call her Ellen. She runs the chemistry side at a lab like NSL. She starts the day with the queue. Forty-odd sample sets in progress, a few of them marked rush. Two customers have emailed overnight asking where their results are. Three new quote requests have arrived, one for a standard package and two for unusual materials that need a chemist's view.

**NORA:** So before she touches science, she's doing customer service.

**JAMES:** Exactly. She answers the status emails by checking with the bench. She prices the standard quote from a spreadsheet and forwards the two unusual ones. Then an instrument flags a calibration check that needs attention, so she reorganises the day's runs. Mid-morning, a rush job for an aerospace customer arrives with an incomplete submission form, so someone has to phone the customer before it can start.

**NORA:** And the afternoon?

**JAMES:** Report review. Her senior chemists have prepared a stack of certificates, and Ellen or another authorised signatory reviews each one against the raw data and the specification before signing. That's the most important thing she does all day, and it's squeezed between everything else.

**NORA:** So where would AI help Ellen?

**JAMES:** In my view, almost everywhere except the signature. A portal would answer the status questions. Instant quotes would handle the standard request. Intake checks would catch the incomplete form before the sample shipped. Drafted reports with flagged exceptions would let her spend her review time on the results that actually need attention, instead of re-checking every routine value by eye. She'd still sign every report. She'd just get more of her day back for the judgement only she can provide.

### The market and the competitors

**NORA:** Let's widen out. How big is this market?

**JAMES:** We didn't find a reliable market size for NSL's specific niche. The nearest figure is a research firm headline, from MarketsandMarkets, saying the aerospace testing market will be worth six point six eight billion dollars by 2029. We didn't read the methodology, and aerospace testing in that sense likely includes a lot more than materials chemistry. So treat it as a sign that the broader market is in the billions, not as NSL's addressable market.

**NORA:** What drives demand?

**JAMES:** Aerospace and defence production and supply-chain qualification, which needs accredited materials data. Additive manufacturing, as more metal parts get printed and need qualifying. Battery materials, as the electric vehicle supply chain needs testing. And potentially nuclear, given the content NSL is publishing. Those are the drivers the company itself points to.

**NORA:** Who does NSL compete with?

**JAMES:** The big names first. Element Materials Technology is a global testing group with a much larger footprint. It was bought by Temasek, the Singapore investment company, from Bridgepoint, and it has restructured to focus on aerospace testing. There's also a report from 2026 that Element was divesting its North American life sciences testing business, which fits that narrower focus. So Element is a direct and much bigger competitor in exactly NSL's core market.

**NORA:** Others?

**JAMES:** Eurofins, the publicly listed testing group, has a materials and engineering sciences business that grew through acquisitions, including EAG Laboratories in 2017. Intertek, another listed testing and certification group, opened a new materials testing lab in Plymouth, Michigan in 2026, competing for US aerospace and automotive materials work. And Lucideon, a UK-based materials testing and consultancy firm, which markets what it calls intelligent testing.

**NORA:** So NSL is a mid-sized independent among giants.

**JAMES:** That's the picture. And that's not necessarily a bad place to be. Large groups have scale and global reach. A focused independent can be more responsive, more specialised, and closer to the customer. Many aerospace suppliers like working with a lab where they know the chemists by name.

**NORA:** You also mentioned software players in your notes.

**JAMES:** Yes, and they're a different kind of competitor. Lab information management systems, usually called LIMS, are the software labs use to track samples, tests and results. Vendors like CloudLIMS, which talks about an AI-native LIMS for environmental labs, and Confident LIMS, which writes about AI in lab data management, are pushing AI into lab workflow and reporting. They don't compete with NSL for testing work. But they change the baseline. If AI-enabled reporting becomes standard in lab software, a lab that still does it by hand falls behind on cost and speed.

**NORA:** And the industry trend overall?

**JAMES:** Consolidation into multi-site platforms. Element and Eurofins built scale through acquisitions, and NSL's own deals follow the same pattern on a smaller scale. A consulting firm's 2026 lab informatics trends piece also points to AI moving into lab data and reporting. So the two trends are scale and digitisation, and NSL needs a plan for both.

**NORA:** Let's go back to the newer markets for a moment. How real are nuclear and batteries for a lab like NSL?

**JAMES:** We don't have NSL's revenue mix, so I can't say how big they are for the company. What I can say is that NSL is clearly positioning for them. Holding an NQA-1 quality programme is a meaningful investment, and you don't make it unless you intend to serve nuclear customers. As general background, there's been renewed interest in nuclear power in the United States, including smaller reactor designs, and every one of those supply chains needs qualified materials.

**NORA:** And batteries?

**JAMES:** Battery materials need precise chemistry. The purity of the metals and compounds in a cell affects its performance and safety, so suppliers need reliable analysis. The instruments NSL already runs for aerospace alloys, like ICP for trace elements, are relevant there too. In my view, these adjacent markets are a smart use of an existing capability, though their growth depends on industries that can be volatile.

**NORA:** And what does Intertek opening a lab in Michigan tell you?

**JAMES:** That the big groups see demand for materials testing in the US Midwest, close to automotive and aerospace manufacturing. That's NSL's backyard. It doesn't mean NSL loses customers, but it does mean a well-funded competitor is investing nearby, and NSL has to keep giving customers reasons to stay.

### AI at NSL today

**NORA:** So where is NSL with AI right now?

**JAMES:** We found no public evidence of AI at NSL. The website doesn't mention AI, data analytics or a client portal. Searches didn't turn up AI hires, partnerships or product announcements. Sample intake is a web request form and downloadable submission forms.

**NORA:** Again, absence of evidence.

**JAMES:** Right, and I'll say it every time. A lab like NSL almost certainly runs a LIMS or similar system internally, and the instruments are digital. There may be good internal automation we can't see. We just know AI isn't part of how NSL presents itself, and the customer-facing experience, at least on the website, is quite traditional.

**NORA:** What do you make of the governance side?

**JAMES:** It's stronger than the lack of AI talk suggests. The accreditation stack and export-control compliance mean NSL already runs a disciplined quality and data-handling system. That's not AI governance, but it's the foundation for it. A lab that already controls methods, validates changes and protects controlled data has most of the habits you need to introduce AI responsibly.

**NORA:** So it's starting from a good place on discipline, and a weak place on digital front end.

**JAMES:** That's my read. Strong on the inside, traditional on the outside. And in my view the opportunity is to bring the outside up to the standard of the inside.

**NORA:** What would an AI-ready lab actually need underneath?

**JAMES:** Three layers, in my view. First, instruments connected to the lab system, so results flow in automatically rather than being transcribed. Many modern instruments can export data, but in many labs there's still a human copying numbers from one screen to another. Second, a clean catalogue of methods, specifications and customer requirements in structured form, so a tool knows which limits apply to which job. And third, a controlled environment for processing data, especially for export-controlled work.

**NORA:** And NSL has which of those?

**JAMES:** We can't tell from the outside. The research notes that NSL runs instruments like ICP, XRF, XRD and LCMS-MS, and that connecting their data to reports and portals is the main enabling step. That's our inference about where the work is. Whether NSL has already done some of it, we don't know.

### The challenges

**NORA:** Let's name the challenges. What's hard for NSL, in your view?

**JAMES:** I'd name five. First, scale competition. Element's aerospace focus, and the size of Eurofins and Intertek, put pressure on price and capacity. When a big group opens a new lab in the Midwest, it's competing for the same customers.

**NORA:** Second?

**JAMES:** Labour. Testing depends on skilled technicians and chemists, and lab staffing is a known constraint in the sector, though we didn't find NSL-specific data. Every report needs qualified people to prepare, review and sign it. If you can't hire them, you can't grow.

**NORA:** What about integrating the labs it has bought?

**JAMES:** That's a sixth challenge, really. Each acquired lab comes with its own systems, its own report formats, its own accreditation scope and its own customers. Rocky Mountain brought environmental testing, which is a different discipline with its own methods and regulators. Bringing those into one customer experience and one data platform takes real effort, and until it's done, the group can feel like several labs sharing a name rather than one platform.

**NORA:** Third?

**JAMES:** The digital front end. Request forms and downloadable submission forms work, but they create friction. Missing information, emails to chase status, re-typing. Larger competitors with client portals can offer a smoother experience, and over time that becomes part of how customers choose.

**NORA:** Fourth.

**JAMES:** Concentration. Two sites, both in Cleveland. That creates capacity limits and continuity risk. If one site has a major problem, there isn't another in-house lab to send the work to. That's our inference, but it's a real consideration for customers who depend on fast turnaround.

**NORA:** And fifth?

**JAMES:** Visibility. No named leadership on the website, no public numbers, undated news. That doesn't matter much to a customer who's been using NSL for twenty years. But for recruiting, for winning new customers in new markets like nuclear and batteries, and eventually for telling a story to a future buyer, a clearer public profile would help.

**NORA:** And the AI-specific challenge?

**JAMES:** The pricing model. Testing is largely priced per test or per sample, and that price reflects the labour inside it. If AI cuts the labour in report preparation, competitors may cut prices, and customers may expect it. Labs that stay manual could find themselves undercut by labs that automated. That's our inference, but it's the classic pattern when a labour-heavy service gets automated.

**NORA:** And customers might bring testing in-house?

**JAMES:** That's another possibility. As instruments get cheaper and AI makes interpretation easier, some large manufacturers might do more testing themselves. In my view, the accreditation requirement and the need for independence limit that, especially for qualification work. But it's worth watching.

### Opportunities

**NORA:** Let's talk opportunities. Where would you push first?

**JAMES:** The first and biggest is automated report drafting from instrument data, with technician review and sign-off. Every test ends in a report. The instruments already produce structured data. The report format is controlled and repetitive. And the sign-off step stays exactly where it is. The value is labour hours per report and turnaround time, which also speeds up invoicing.

**NORA:** You can't size it, though.

**JAMES:** No, we didn't find report volumes or headcount, so I won't put a number on it. But in a lab, I'd expect report preparation to be a meaningful share of skilled time. Even a modest cut would free chemists for more testing, which in a labour-constrained business is capacity.

**NORA:** Second?

**JAMES:** Digital quoting from the test catalogue. NSL has a broad menu of standard tests. A customer who needs the usual chemistry package for a common alloy shouldn't have to wait for someone to price it by email. Instant quotes for standard work, with an expert handling the unusual requests. That saves sales and lab-manager time and probably wins more small jobs.

**NORA:** Third?

**JAMES:** A client portal with digital intake and live status. We walked through it with Priya. It reduces errors at intake, cuts status-chasing emails, and makes NSL easier to work with. And it's the front door for everything else, including the insight services I mentioned.

**NORA:** What else?

**JAMES:** Fourth, cross-selling between the two sites. Chemistry and metallurgy often apply to the same parts. A single customer view could show that a chemistry customer never uses NSL for metallurgy, and prompt a conversation. Fifth, pricing on value. Accredited, fast turnaround for critical aerospace programmes is worth paying for, so a clear rush tier makes sense. Sixth, continued acquisitions of regional labs in aerospace or electronics testing, following the pattern of Central Testing and Rocky Mountain. And seventh, cross-selling the environmental testing that came with Rocky Mountain to existing aerospace and industrial customers.

**NORA:** Is there an AI opportunity on the science side, not just the paperwork?

**JAMES:** There could be. Anomaly detection on instrument data, spotting a calibration drift or an unusual pattern early. Helping metallurgists classify microstructure images. These are real uses in the wider industry. But in my view they come later, because they touch the accredited method itself and need careful validation. Start with the paperwork, where the risk is lower and the method is untouched.

**NORA:** And the insight idea you mentioned with Priya. Is that a real business?

**JAMES:** It could be, in my view, though it's unproven. Picture a customer dashboard that shows each customer their own results over time: trends in trace elements across lots, how close they typically run to specification limits, which suppliers' material varies most. For a powder producer or a forging house, that's useful quality intelligence. It could be included to win loyalty, or sold as a premium tier.

**NORA:** With the data kept strictly per customer.

**JAMES:** Strictly. A lab's whole business depends on confidentiality. Customer A must never see customer B's results, and in defence work, some data can't leave controlled systems at all. Any insight product has to be designed around that from the start.

### The best AI bet

**NORA:** If you had to pick one AI bet for the next eighteen months, what is it?

**JAMES:** Report drafting from instrument output. It's the most repetitive, highest-volume skilled task, the data is already digital, and the human sign-off keeps it inside the quality system. And it doesn't require customers to change anything, which means you can start without a big client-facing project.

**NORA:** Give me the first hundred days.

**JAMES:** Days one to thirty: pick one high-volume test family, say a standard chemistry package on common aerospace alloys. Map exactly how a report is produced today, from instrument output to signed certificate, and time each step. Work with the quality manager from day one to decide how the tool will be validated under the lab's accreditations. And agree on where the data will be processed, with export-controlled work kept out of scope or in a fully controlled environment.

**NORA:** You'd bring in quality before you write any code.

**JAMES:** Before anything. In an accredited lab, the quality manager can stop any project, and should. Make them a co-owner. Days thirty to sixty: build the drafting tool for that one test family, pulling values from the instrument and LIMS data, applying specification limits and producing the report in the controlled format. Run it in parallel: chemists produce their normal report and the draft side by side, and you compare every field.

**NORA:** Shadow mode.

**JAMES:** Shadow mode, with a validation record that would satisfy an auditor. Days sixty to a hundred: once the draft matches perfectly over a meaningful number of reports, move to draft-first with human review and sign-off, measure time saved and turnaround, and pick the next test family. By day one hundred you should have a validated tool for one family, real numbers, and a plan for the next three.

**NORA:** What would you measure, specifically?

**JAMES:** Four things. Skilled minutes per report, from data ready to report signed. Turnaround time, from sample received to report issued. First-time-right rate, meaning how often a report goes out without a correction later. And the number of fields the reviewer had to change on the AI draft, which tells you whether the tool is actually getting better. If the first three improve and the fourth heads toward zero, you have a case to scale.

**NORA:** And what would make you stop?

**JAMES:** Any sign that review quality is slipping. If reviewers start signing drafts faster without actually checking, the tool has made the lab worse, not better. That's why I'd keep periodic blind checks, where a reviewer gets a draft with a deliberate error and you see whether they catch it. It sounds harsh, but it's how you keep human sign-off meaningful.

**NORA:** Who owns it?

**JAMES:** A lab operations leader with deep testing credibility, paired with the quality manager. Not an outside technology team working alone. Chemists need to trust that the tool was built by people who understand the method.

**NORA:** And what about the people whose job this changes?

**JAMES:** Be clear from the start that the goal is to move skilled people from typing to judgement and to more testing, not to cut them. In a labour-constrained industry, that's genuinely true, and it should be said. Involve senior chemists in the design and let them own the validation. The best way to get adoption is to let the experts make the tool better.

**NORA:** And the second-best bet?

**JAMES:** Instant quoting and a client portal. It's more visible to customers and may win new business, but it's a bigger project with more moving parts, so it comes second.

### Lessons for other businesses

**NORA:** Let's step back. What can other businesses learn from NSL?

**JAMES:** Four lessons. First, find the document that is your product. In many service businesses, the thing the customer actually receives is a document: a report, a certificate, an assessment. If that document is produced from structured data by skilled people following a standard format, it's a prime candidate for AI drafting with human sign-off.

**NORA:** Second?

**JAMES:** Second, regulation and accreditation aren't reasons to wait. They're reasons to be careful and to start with the quality team. A disciplined organisation that validates changes can introduce AI more safely than a looser one. The discipline you already have is an asset.

**NORA:** Third?

**JAMES:** Third, fix the front door. Customers judge you on how easy you are to work with, not just on the quality of the result. Quoting, intake and status are where friction lives. A portal isn't glamorous, but it changes the relationship.

**NORA:** And fourth?

**JAMES:** Fourth, think about pricing before your competitors do. If your price reflects labour and AI reduces the labour, someone will eventually cut prices. Decide in advance how you'll compete: faster turnaround, premium rush tiers, insight services, or a portal that makes you the easiest lab to use. Don't let the competitor who automates first set your price.

**NORA:** I'd add one more. Your history of data is an asset.

**JAMES:** Yes. A lab with decades of results has something unique. Not to share across customers, that would breach trust, but to offer each customer insight into their own trends. Many businesses sit on years of data they've only used once.

### Risks and what to watch

**NORA:** Let's talk risks.

**JAMES:** One, AI disruption to pricing. If report drafting and data review become automated across the industry, the labour-based price of a report falls, and manual labs lose on price. Two, scale competitors. Element's focus on aerospace and the expansion of Intertek and Eurofins put pressure on NSL's core. Three, customers insourcing some testing as instruments and AI get cheaper. Four, technician labour constraints limiting growth.

**NORA:** And AI-specific risks inside the lab?

**JAMES:** Accuracy and validation. An AI-drafted report with one wrong number is a serious problem in aerospace. The defence is designing the tool to pull values directly from instrument data rather than generating them, validating it thoroughly, and keeping human sign-off. And data control. Export-controlled data must stay where it's allowed to be. A careless AI deployment that sent controlled data to the wrong place would be far worse than no AI at all.

**NORA:** And for the owners?

**JAMES:** Levine Leichtman invested in mid-2024, so it's a little over two years into the hold. The value story at exit will rest on growth, margins and the quality of the platform. A lab that can show faster turnaround, higher capacity per chemist, a modern client experience and a validated approach to AI is a much more attractive asset than one that looks like it did in 2015.

**NORA:** What should listeners watch?

**JAMES:** Three things. First, any announcement of a client portal or digital intake at NSL. Second, more acquisitions, especially into new regions or capabilities. And third, any public statement about AI or automation in reporting, ideally framed around accreditation and data security. If NSL talks about how it uses AI safely inside its quality system, that's a sign of maturity.

### Quick-fire round

**NORA:** Quick-fire round. Short answers.

**JAMES:** Go.

**NORA:** What does NSL sell?

**JAMES:** Trusted, accredited answers about what a material is and how it behaves.

**NORA:** Most valuable asset?

**JAMES:** Its accreditation stack and eighty years of reputation.

**NORA:** Biggest weakness?

**JAMES:** A traditional digital front end, and a thin public profile.

**NORA:** Shipped AI feature?

**JAMES:** None that we found.

**NORA:** Best AI bet?

**JAMES:** Drafting test reports from instrument data, with human review and sign-off.

**NORA:** Will AI replace the chemist?

**JAMES:** No. It will replace the copying, and leave the chemist more time for the science.

**NORA:** One thing an aerospace quality manager should ask their lab this year?

**JAMES:** Can I get my results as structured data, not just a document?

**NORA:** Optimist or pessimist?

**JAMES:** Optimist. The moat is real. The question is whether NSL modernises before a bigger competitor uses AI to undercut it.

### Wrap-up

**NORA:** Let me try a summary. NSL Analytical Services is a Cleveland testing lab founded in 1945, with chemistry and metallurgy sites serving aerospace, defence, additive manufacturing, batteries, power and nuclear customers. It was bought by May River Capital around 2020 and then by Levine Leichtman in mid-2024, and it has added labs including Central Testing and Rocky Mountain Testing Solutions. Its moat is an accreditation stack, Nadcap, ISO 17025, NQA-1 and export-control compliance, that new entrants can't easily copy. It competes with much larger groups like Element, Eurofins and Intertek, and we found no public evidence of AI. The best opportunity, in our view, is AI drafting of test reports from instrument data, validated with the quality team and signed by a human, followed by instant quoting and a client portal. The risk is that competitors automate first and reset the price of a report.

**JAMES:** That's it. And the lesson that travels is simple. When the report is the product, make the report faster without ever making it less trustworthy. Do that, and the moat gets wider, not narrower.
